content: Angina refers to chest pain or discomfort that arises when the heart muscle does not receive an adequate supply of blood. This pain is often described as a sensation of pressure or squeezing in the chest. It may also radiate to the shoulders, arms, neck, jaw, or back. In some cases, it can mimic the feeling of indigestion. Angina is not a disease itself but rather a symptom of coronary artery disease (CAD), which is the most common type of heart disease. CAD occurs when fatty deposits, known as plaque, accumulate in the coronary arteries, reducing blood flow. This diminished blood flow prevents the heart from receiving sufficient oxygen-rich blood, leading to angina. Symptoms of Angina The hallmark symptom of angina is chest pain, which serves as a critical indicator of coronary artery disease and myocardial ischemia. However, other symptoms may accompany angina, including: Chest pain: This is typically localized to the precordial region or behind the sternum. It is important to note that not all chest pain is related to coronary artery disease. Chest pressure: Some individuals describe this as a sensation of a heavy weight or a tight band around the chest. Indigestion-like symptoms: These may include loss of appetite, nausea, or vomiting in some patients. Pain radiating to other areas: Discomfort may extend to the shoulders, arms, jaw, or back, often accompanying chest pain. It is essential to recognize that other health conditions can cause similar symptoms. Only a healthcare professional can accurately diagnose the underlying cause. Anyone experiencing these symptoms should consult a doctor promptly to ensure early diagnosis and treatment. Risk Factors for Angina Several factors can increase the likelihood of developing angina, many of which overlap with the risk factors for coronary artery disease. These risk factors can be categorized into modifiable and non-modifiable groups: Modifiable Risk Factors Cigarette smoking: Smoking significantly increases the risk of coronary heart disease, with smokers being 2–4 times more likely to develop the condition compared to non-smokers. Smoking also heightens the risk of sudden cardiac death and interacts with other risk factors to amplify the danger. High blood cholesterol: Elevated cholesterol levels, particularly LDL cholesterol, are strongly associated with an increased risk of coronary artery disease. Diet plays a significant role in cholesterol levels. Stress: Chronic stress can contribute to coronary artery disease by promoting unhealthy behaviors such as overeating or smoking. Obesity: A high body mass index (BMI), particularly above 28, is a risk factor for angina. Weight management can help reduce this risk. High blood pressure: Hypertension increases the risk of coronary artery disease by reducing the coronary arteries' reserve capacity. Diabetes mellitus: Diabetes damages both coronary arteries and myocardial capillaries, increasing the risk of coronary artery disease. Excessive alcohol consumption: Overconsumption of alcohol can harm the arteries and myocardium. Non-Modifiable Risk Factors Age: Individuals over the age of 65 are at a higher risk of developing coronary artery disease. Gender: Men are at a greater risk than women, although post-menopausal women also face an increased risk compared to younger women. Family history: A family history of cardiovascular diseases increases the likelihood of developing coronary artery disease. Race: African Americans are at a higher risk compared to other racial groups. Diagnosis of Angina Since other health conditions can mimic the symptoms of angina, it is crucial to seek medical evaluation for an accurate diagnosis. Diagnostic tests may include: Electrocardiogram (ECG): This painless test measures the heart's electrical activity to detect abnormalities or irregular heart rhythms. Echocardiogram: This imaging test identifies areas of the heart that may not be contracting normally. Blood tests: Tests such as CK-MB and troponin levels can help determine if the heart has sustained damage. Coronary angiography: This imaging procedure involves injecting a special dye into the coronary arteries to visualize blockages on X-rays. Stress testing: Conducted during physical exertion, this test helps identify heart disease more effectively. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care Individuals with a family history of cardiovascular diseases or unhealthy lifestyle habits should regularly consult their doctor for follow-up care. Immediate medical attention is necessary if any of the following symptoms occur: Persistent and severe chest pain Sudden drop in blood pressure Shortness of breath Angina or chest pain accompanied by sweating, nausea, or discomfort in the shoulders, arms, jaw, neck, or abdomen These symptoms may indicate acute coronary syndrome (ACS), requiring urgent hospital evaluation. Treatment Options for Angina Treatment for angina includes general lifestyle modifications, medications, and interventional or surgical procedures. The choice of treatment depends on the severity of symptoms and the degree of coronary artery stenosis. A doctor will discuss the available options, expected outcomes, and potential side effects to develop a personalized treatment plan. General Therapy Weight and waistline management Smoking and alcohol cessation Regular physical activity Stress management Medications Anti-platelet drugs: Aspirin (75–100 mg daily) is beneficial for most patients with stable angina. Alternatives like clopidogrel or prasugrel may be used for those with peptic ulcers. Beta-blockers: These reduce heart rate, myocardial contractility, and catecholamine toxicity. Commonly used agents include metoprolol, bisoprolol, and nebivolol. Beta-blockers are contraindicated in patients with asthma, severe conduction block, or heart failure. Nitroglycerin (NG): This vasodilator improves myocardial ischemia and is available in various forms, including sublingual sprays and transdermal patches. Side effects may include headache, hypotension, and facial flushing. Calcium-channel blockers: These reduce myocardial oxygen demand and reverse coronary vasospasm. Verapamil and gallopamil are commonly used, with bradycardia as a potential side effect. ACE inhibitors: Drugs like enalapril and ramipril improve heart failure symptoms and prognosis. Side effects include dry cough and angioedema. Patients intolerant to ACE inhibitors may switch to angiotensin II receptor antagonists. Statins: These cholesterol-lowering agents reduce LDL cholesterol and increase HDL cholesterol. Common drugs include atorvastatin and lovastatin. Side effects may include liver enzyme abnormalities and muscle cramps. Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI) PCI is a minimally invasive procedure performed in a cardiac catheterization lab to reopen blocked coronary arteries. A catheter with a deflated balloon is inserted into the diseased artery, and the balloon is inflated to restore blood flow. A stent may be placed to keep the artery open. PCI is highly effective and safe for improving angina symptoms. Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG) CABG is a surgical procedure that reroutes blood flow around a blocked artery using healthy blood vessels from the patient’s body, such as the leg or chest wall. Post-surgery, patients are advised to adopt a low-fat, low-cholesterol diet and engage in regular physical activity to strengthen the heart and prevent further blockages. Where to Seek Medical Care for Angina Patients should consult hospitals or specialized centers for the treatment of angina. Early diagnosis and management are crucial to prevent complications. Diseases with Similar Symptoms Other conditions may mimic angina symptoms, necessitating thorough evaluation by a healthcare provider. These include: Shortness of breath: May be caused by respiratory conditions like pneumonitis or pulmonary tuberculosis. Indigestion: Could indicate digestive disorders such as gastritis or peptic ulcers. Pain in shoulders, arms, jaw, or back: May result from conditions like scapulohumeral periarthritis or dental issues.
